articles.label: Investigation
articles.headline: Escambia County's $2.3M tourism contract renewed without competitive bid
articles.dek: The county commission quietly extended its marketing agreement with a Tallahassee firm last week. Three commissioners had received campaign contributions from the firm's lobbyist.
brief: Escambia County commissioners voted 4-1 to extend a $2.3 million tourism marketing contract with Tallahassee-based Coastal Strategies Group without issuing a competitive bid
Campaign finance records show three of the four commissioners who voted yes received contributions from the firm's registered lobbyist within the past 18 months
The sole dissenting vote came from Commissioner Mike Kohler, who called the process 'a textbook example of why people don't trust local government'
articles.body:
The agenda item appeared on page 47 of a 52-page packet. No presentation. No discussion period. Just a consent vote lumped in with routine contracts for janitorial services and fleet maintenance.

That's how Escambia County renewed a $2.3 million tourism marketing contract last Thursday evening—extending its agreement with Coastal Strategies Group for another three years without ever asking another firm to compete for the work.

Four commissioners voted yes. One voted no. The whole thing took less than ninety seconds.

What the public record doesn't show: three of those four yes votes came from commissioners who received campaign contributions from David Harrington, Coastal Strategies' registered lobbyist with Escambia County. The contributions totaled $7,500 across the three campaigns over the past 18 months, according to campaign finance disclosures filed with the Escambia County Supervisor of Elections.

The contract

Coastal Strategies Group has held Escambia County's tourism marketing contract since 2019. The firm handles digital advertising, social media management, and promotional campaigns for Visit Pensacola, the county's destination marketing organization.

The original contract was awarded through a competitive procurement process. Three firms submitted proposals. Coastal Strategies won.

This renewal was different.

County purchasing policy allows contract extensions without competitive bidding under certain conditions—when services are deemed "specialized" or when switching vendors would cause "significant disruption." Staff invoked both justifications in a two-paragraph memo attached to the agenda item.

"Coastal Strategies Group has developed institutional knowledge of the Pensacola tourism market and established relationships with regional media outlets," the memo stated. "A transition to a new vendor would result in loss of continuity during the peak tourism season."

The renewal extends the contract through September 2029 at the same annual rate: approximately $767,000 per year.

The contributions

David Harrington registered as a lobbyist with Escambia County in March 2024, listing Coastal Strategies Group as his sole client. State lobbying records show he is a principal at Harrington Government Relations, a Tallahassee firm with municipal and county clients across North Florida.

Campaign finance records tell the rest of the story.

Commissioner Lumon May received $3,000 from Harrington in October 2024, during his reelection campaign. Commissioner Jeff Bergosh received $2,500 in February 2025. Commissioner Steven Barry received $2,000 in August 2025.

All three voted to extend the contract.

Commissioner Doug Underhill, who also voted yes, did not receive contributions from Harrington. He did not respond to requests for comment.

The Flightline reached out to all four commissioners who voted for the renewal. May and Bergosh did not respond. Barry, through a spokesperson, said the contribution had "no bearing whatsoever" on his vote.

"Commissioner Barry evaluates every contract on its merits," the statement read. "Coastal Strategies has delivered results for Escambia County tourism, and continuity of service was the deciding factor."

Harrington also did not respond to a request for comment.

The dissent

Commissioner Mike Kohler was the only no vote.

He didn't speak during the meeting—consent items rarely generate discussion—but he had plenty to say afterward.

"This is a textbook example of why people don't trust local government," Kohler said in an interview Monday. "We're talking about $2.3 million of public money, and we can't be bothered to see if someone else might do it better or cheaper? That's not how you run a $500 million budget."

Kohler said he reviewed the agenda item before the meeting and flagged concerns to county staff. He asked whether other firms had expressed interest in the contract. Staff told him they hadn't solicited interest.

"That's the whole point," Kohler said. "You don't know who's interested if you don't ask."

Kohler said he was unaware of the campaign contributions until The Flightline brought them to his attention. He declined to speculate on whether they influenced his colleagues' votes.

"I'm not going to accuse anyone of anything," he said. "But the optics are terrible. And in local government, optics matter."

What the law says

Florida law does not prohibit elected officials from voting on matters involving their campaign contributors. Unlike federal law, which bars certain contractor contributions to officials overseeing their contracts, state law places no such restrictions on county commissioners.

The Florida Commission on Ethics has issued advisory opinions stating that campaign contributions alone do not create a voting conflict under state ethics statutes. A conflict requires a "special private gain or loss"—a standard courts have interpreted narrowly.

County policy is similarly permissive. Escambia County's code of ethics requires disclosure of conflicts involving direct financial interests but does not address campaign contributions.

Robert Holley, a government accountability attorney in Tallahassee, said the arrangement is legal but problematic.

"You're operating in that gray zone where everything is technically above board, but reasonable people would question it," Holley said. "When you've got a lobbyist giving money to commissioners and then those commissioners voting to give his client a multimillion-dollar contract without competition, that's a story that writes itself."

The tourism numbers

Visit Pensacola reported 6.2 million visitors to Escambia County in 2025, generating an estimated $3.1 billion in economic impact. Those figures are up slightly from 2024 and represent a full recovery from pandemic-era declines.

The organization credits its marketing campaigns—run by Coastal Strategies—for driving the growth. A presentation to the Tourist Development Council in January cited increased engagement on social media, higher click-through rates on digital ads, and expanded coverage in regional travel publications.

Whether another firm could deliver similar or better results at the same price is unknowable. The county never asked.

Visit Pensacola Executive Director Lori Comer declined to comment on the contract renewal, referring questions to county administration.

County Administrator Wes Moreno said the decision to forgo competitive bidding was made by the purchasing department based on established policy.

"We followed the rules," Moreno said. "The contract has performed well. There was no requirement to rebid."

Asked whether the campaign contributions raised concerns, Moreno said that was "a question for the commissioners."

What happens next

The contract is now active. Coastal Strategies will continue its work through at least September 2029.

Kohler said he plans to propose changes to county purchasing policy that would require competitive bidding for all contracts above $500,000, regardless of extension provisions. He acknowledged the proposal faces long odds.

"I'll probably lose 4-1," he said. "But at least it'll be on the record."

The next Escambia County Commission meeting is scheduled for August 7.

articles.label: Development
articles.headline: Downtown Pensacola's empty storefronts: A block-by-block count
articles.dek: Six months after the city touted its urban revival, Palafox Street has 14 vacant ground-floor spaces between Garden and Main. Business owners say parking and rent are killing foot traffic.
brief: A Flightline survey found 14 vacant ground-floor commercial spaces along Palafox Street between Garden and Main streets
Business owners cite parking scarcity and rising rents—some reaching $35 per square foot—as primary obstacles to foot traffic and tenant retention
The vacancy count contradicts the city's January announcement celebrating downtown's 'renaissance' and 94% occupancy rate
articles.body:
The paper sign in the window at 24 South Palafox has been there since March. "Thanks for 12 great years," it reads. "We'll miss you, Pensacola." The boutique that occupied the space is now in Gulf Breeze. The 1,800-square-foot storefront remains empty.

Walk three blocks north and you'll count six more just like it. Vacant. For lease. Coming soon—but not yet.

A Flightline survey conducted over two days last week documented 14 empty ground-floor commercial spaces along Palafox Street between Garden Street and Main Street. That's roughly one in eight storefronts on downtown Pensacola's primary corridor sitting dark on a summer weekend.

The count comes six months after city officials announced at a January press conference that downtown was experiencing a "renaissance," citing a 94% commercial occupancy rate and record permit applications for new businesses.

The Numbers

The Flightline walked both sides of Palafox from Garden to Main on July 25 and 26, photographing and cataloging every ground-floor commercial space. The survey counted only street-level retail and restaurant spaces, excluding upper-floor offices, residential units and parking structures.

The results:

  • Garden to Romana: 3 vacant spaces
  • Romana to Intendencia: 4 vacant spaces
  • Intendencia to Government: 2 vacant spaces
  • Government to Main: 5 vacant spaces

Of the 14 vacancies, nine had "For Lease" signs with contact information. Three had no signage at all. Two displayed "Coming Soon" notices—one dated November 2025.

The city's January figure appears to have used a different methodology. Downtown Improvement Board executive director Marcus Webb said the 94% rate included upper-floor office space and measured the entire Downtown Improvement Board district, which extends well beyond Palafox.

"Ground-floor retail is always going to be more volatile than office space," Webb said by phone Thursday. "We're still seeing strong interest from prospective tenants."

'The rent is insane'

Teresa Coolidge has operated a gift shop on South Palafox for nine years. She asked that the shop not be named because she's currently negotiating her lease renewal.

"The rent is insane," she said, standing behind her counter on a Tuesday afternoon. Two customers browsed the shelves. "I'm paying $28 a square foot. My landlord wants $35 for the new lease. That's a 25% increase."

Commercial real estate listings reviewed by The Flightline show asking rents along Palafox ranging from $24 to $38 per square foot for ground-floor retail, depending on the block. A decade ago, rates averaged $14 to $18 per square foot, according to archived listings from LoopNet.

Property owners counter that their costs have risen too. Insurance premiums for commercial buildings in downtown Pensacola increased an average of 47% between 2023 and 2025, according to data from the Florida Office of Insurance Regulation. Property taxes in the Community Redevelopment Area have climbed alongside assessed values.

"I'm not getting rich off these buildings," said one property owner who asked not to be named because he has tenants. "I've got a mortgage, I've got insurance, I've got maintenance. The margins aren't what people think."

The parking problem

Every business owner interviewed for this story mentioned parking within the first two minutes.

"I watch people circle the block three times and then leave," said James Okonkwo, who co-owns a restaurant on North Palafox. "That's a customer I'll never see again. They're going to Tiger Point or Cordova Mall, where they can park right in front."

Downtown Pensacola has roughly 4,200 public parking spaces across surface lots, garages and street parking, according to the Downtown Improvement Board. On weekday afternoons and weekend evenings, finding a spot within two blocks of Palafox can require 10 to 15 minutes of circling.

The city added 280 spaces when it opened the Jefferson Street garage in 2024. But business owners say the garage, located three blocks east of Palafox, is too far to help retail foot traffic.

"Nobody's going to park three blocks away to browse a boutique," Coolidge said. "They'll do it for a nice dinner. They won't do it to buy a candle."

City Councilwoman Sherri Myers, whose district includes downtown, acknowledged the parking issue at a council meeting earlier this month.

"We need to be honest about the trade-offs," Myers said. "We wanted a walkable downtown. We wanted outdoor dining. We wanted bike lanes. Those things took parking spaces. I'm not saying we were wrong, but we need to deal with the consequences."

What the vacancies look like

Not all empty storefronts are equal. Some are clearly between tenants—freshly painted, well-maintained, with active listing information. Others suggest longer-term problems.

The former home of a women's clothing store on the 100 block of South Palafox has been vacant since January 2025. The windows are papered over. The listing, according to a broker contacted by The Flightline, has been pulled. The owner is "evaluating options."

Two doors down, a space that once held a home goods store has been empty since the store relocated to East Hill in 2024. The owner, a limited liability company registered in Delaware, did not respond to requests for comment.

At the corner of Palafox and Government, the ground floor of a recently renovated mixed-use building has never been occupied. The building opened in late 2023. The retail space has been listed at $36 per square foot since then.

"That corner should be gold," said Rick Barton, a commercial real estate agent not involved in the listing. "The fact that it's sat empty for two and a half years tells you something's off. Either the rent's too high or the space doesn't work. Probably both."

The city's response

The Flightline submitted questions to the city's communications office on July 24 regarding the vacancy rate, parking policy and any planned interventions for struggling retail corridors.

A spokesperson responded Thursday with a statement: "Downtown Pensacola remains a vibrant destination with strong interest from businesses and developers. The city continues to work with the Downtown Improvement Board and private property owners to maintain a healthy commercial environment."

The statement did not address specific questions about vacancy rates or parking.

The Downtown Improvement Board's Webb said his organization is working on several initiatives, including a facade improvement grant program and negotiations with private lot owners to expand public parking availability. He declined to provide specifics, citing ongoing discussions.

What comes next

The vacant spaces along Palafox tell different stories. Some will fill within months. Others may sit empty for years. A few could be converted to residential or office use, as has happened elsewhere downtown.

For now, they're a visible counterpoint to the city's optimistic narrative.

"I want downtown to succeed," said Okonkwo, the restaurant owner. "I moved my business here because I believed in it. But you can't just say everything's fine when people can see with their own eyes that it's not."

He gestured out the window toward South Palafox, where a customer walked past an empty storefront without stopping.

"Count the dark windows," he said. "That's the story."

articles.label: Military
articles.headline: NAS Pensacola's summer surge: 800 new flight students and a housing crunch
articles.dek: The Blue Angels aren't the only thing in the sky. A record class of naval aviators is stretching base capacity and spilling into Gulf Breeze rentals, changing the neighborhood calculus for year-round residents.
brief: Naval Air Station Pensacola welcomed approximately 800 new student naval aviators this summer, the largest incoming class in over a decade
On-base housing shortfall has pushed an estimated 200 students into the private rental market, with Gulf Breeze and East Hill absorbing most of the overflow
Year-round residents report increased competition for rentals and rising lease prices, while landlords navigate the unusual rhythms of military tenant turnover
articles.body:
At 6:15 on a Tuesday morning, the T-6B Texan IIs are already climbing out over Escambia Bay. From the deck of a house on Shoreline Drive in Gulf Breeze, you can count them. Three. Four. A fifth banking east toward the practice area. By 7 a.m., the sky will be full.

This is the sound of Naval Air Station Pensacola operating at surge capacity.

The base welcomed approximately 800 new student naval aviators this summer, according to figures provided by Naval Air Training Command public affairs. It's the largest incoming class since 2012, when the Navy was ramping down from wartime operations. This time, the surge is about rebuilding.

"We're making up for several years of reduced throughput," said Lt. Cmdr. Marcus Webb, a public affairs officer at NAS Pensacola. "The fleet needs pilots. That's the bottom line."

The bottom line has a housing problem.

Beds and billets

NAS Pensacola's on-base housing was designed for a smaller student population. Bachelor officer quarters can accommodate roughly 600 students at a time, according to base housing officials. With 800 new arrivals joining students already mid-pipeline, the math doesn't work.

Webb confirmed that approximately 200 students are currently authorized to live off-base and receive a basic allowance for housing. That's money in someone's pocket. The question is whose.

In Gulf Breeze, the answer is increasingly: landlords who once catered to tourists and snowbirds.

"I had a two-bedroom on Fairpoint that I used to rent weekly in summer, monthly in winter," said Dana Krebs, who owns three rental properties in Gulf Breeze proper. "Now I've got a Navy lieutenant on a 10-month lease. Steady income. No cleaning turnover every Saturday. It's a different business model."

Krebs said she raised the monthly rent by $200 when her last seasonal tenant moved out in April. The Navy student who signed in May didn't blink.

"They get that housing allowance," she said. "They know what they can spend."

The neighborhood math

For year-round Gulf Breeze residents who rent rather than own, the calculation is less favorable.

Michelle Tran has lived in the same Fairpoint Drive apartment complex for four years. When her lease came up for renewal in June, her landlord proposed a $275 monthly increase.

"He told me straight up," Tran said. "He said he could get more from Navy students. They're guaranteed to pay. I'm a substitute teacher."

Tran negotiated the increase down to $150. She's looking for other options but finding few. The vacancy rate in Gulf Breeze has been tight for years, driven by the same forces reshaping Pensacola's market: remote workers, retirees and a building pace that hasn't matched demand.

Now add 200 flight students with housing stipends.

Escambia County property records and rental listings reviewed by The Flightline show asking rents in Gulf Breeze up an average of 8% since January 2026, outpacing the county-wide average of 5.2%. The data doesn't isolate the Navy's impact, but rental agents say the correlation is obvious.

"When I get a listing in the $1,400 to $1,800 range, I know it's going to a student or a contractor," said Reyes Suárez, a leasing agent with Pensacola Beach Realty who handles Gulf Breeze properties. "Families looking for a three-bedroom? They're going to Pace or Milton."

The pipeline

Student naval aviators at Pensacola are in the early stages of a training pipeline that will eventually send them to Corpus Christi, Kingsville, Meridian or other advanced training sites. Time in Pensacola ranges from six months to over a year, depending on aircraft track and training availability.

That creates a steady churn. A student who signed a lease in May might be gone by January. Another will take the unit in February. The landlord doesn't care. The neighbor might.

"They're fine kids, don't get me wrong," said Harold Boudreaux, who lives next door to a rental on Navy Cove Road that has housed three different student aviators since 2024. "But there's no continuity. They don't come to the neighborhood association. They're not picking up after the hurricanes. They're here to fly, and then they're gone."

Boudreaux said he's not complaining, exactly. He served in the Navy himself, stationed at Pensacola in 1987. He understands the mission.

"I just notice it," he said. "The neighborhood feels different."

Base response

Navy officials say they're aware of the off-base housing pressure and are exploring options. A base housing study completed in 2024 recommended construction of additional bachelor quarters, but funding hasn't been allocated.

"We work with community partners to ensure our sailors have quality housing options," Webb said. "We also encourage our students to be good neighbors."

The Navy's community liaison office has distributed informational packets to students living off-base, covering topics from trash collection schedules to noise ordinances. Whether that translates to attendance at neighborhood association meetings remains to be seen.

Meanwhile, the T-6Bs keep climbing. The runway at NAS Pensacola recorded 847 training sorties last week, according to flight operations data. That's up from 612 during the same week last year.

The Blue Angels may be what tourists come to see. But the real air traffic is wearing student wings.

And it needs somewhere to sleep.
